documents.unit: Siebel School of Computing and Data Science
documents.title: AI in CS 124
documents.summary: Course-level position statement explaining why the intro course has embraced AI coding agents, requiring them (Claude Code) on an individual independent project while keeping AI banned on proctored quizzes that carry most of the grade. It gives rationale (career relevance, non-majors), describes scaffolding for AI-supported work, cost and equity notes, and an FAQ that clarifies scope and responsibility for validating AI-generated code.

Employers expect graduates to know these skills.
We will continue to prohibit AI use on our proctored quizzes
CS 124 only teaches AI-supported programming on the independent project.
you are still responsible for validating all the code in your project.
speak to Geoff if this amount represents a barrier to your success
we will continue to monitor student performance in CS 124 and in later
This policy only applies to CS 124.

documents.unit: Siebel School of Computing and Data Science
documents.title: CS 124: Fall 2026 Syllabus
documents.summary: Syllabus that splits the course into two regimes: homework and quizzes where all code must be the student's own (AI may explain concepts but not produce code), and an independent project where an AI coding agent is expected to write most code and grading is based on logged hours of engaged work. It redefines integrity violations for the project around session logs, describes automated checks, and adds a responsible-AI section on differing policies elsewhere and AI's costs.

asking questions is fine, getting answers is not.
an AI coding agent will write most of your code, and we expect it to.
Your project grade is based on the total hours of engaged work you complete

We will run automated checks on reported session activity, session transcripts, and code changes.

they consume enormous resources, they were trained on data collected without consent

documents.title: EECS 280 Syllabus
documents.summary: The EECS 280 syllabus ties generative AI and AI-assisted editors to the course's collaboration rules: AI may be used only where help from another person would be allowed. A two-column table lists allowed uses (learning concepts, understanding compiler errors, brainstorming edge cases, practice questions) and prohibited ones (generating submitted code or tests, exhaustive proofreading, exams), plus a ban on deceptive or malicious AI use; suspected violations go to the Engineering Honor Council.
